scope: The Union defence budget FY2000-01 → FY2026-27 as the Ministry of Defence's demands for grants print it: Defence Services (Revenue) with the Army, Navy, Air Force, Ordnance (OFB, then Directorate of Ordnance) and R&D heads and their Pay & Allowances lines; Capital Outlay on Defence Services with its service totals (where printed) and main categories; Defence Pensions by service; MoD Civil including the Coast Guard, the Border Roads Development Board and Defence Estates — BE, RE and actuals for every FY the fetched documents give (every FY has a BE; actuals for 2009-10, 2012-13, 2014-15, 2016-17, 2018-19, 2020-21, 2022-23, 2024-25). Entities: the ministry, the services, DRDO, IDS, BRO, Coast Guard, DGDE, the pension demand, OFB and its seven successors, the eight listed DPSUs, and the Defence Ministers 2000–2026 as dated roles. Base rates: the four-demand total against GDP and against total Union expenditure, pension and capital shares, and SIPRI's peer set. Three levels of resolution: Union money resolves to the line item; state money resolves to the Police major head per state (and prisons per state from NCRB), with strength and per-capita figures reported: while BPR&D is down; city money does not exist outside Delhi Police, and city strength has no primary while BPR&D is down — cities get the footprint (installations, commissionerate entities with reported: strength) and the void. This file carries only the Union level; it leaves out procurement awards, DPSU order books, pay scales, Agnipath/OROP terms, the cases and the footprint, which sit in sibling files.

entities.publicRole: The payer for every rupee in this file; the demands it carries are the Union defence budget.
d: Actual 2024-25, four demands summed: ₹636,003.01 crore (revenue 290,964.51; capital 159,768.40; pensions 157,653.65; civil 27,616.45) [documented]
BE 2026-27, four demands summed: ₹784,678.28 crore = 2.00% of projected GDP and 14.7% of total Union expenditure (BE) [documented]

Demand numbers shift by year: Demands 13–19 in 2001-02; 21–28 in 2005-06; 20–27 (one demand per service) 2009-10 to 2015-16; 20–23 (merged) in 2016-17; 19–22 from 2017-18 except 18–21 in 2019-20 to 2021-22; every budgets row names its demand [documented]

Department of Defence Production, value of production FY2023-24: DPSUs ₹74,434 crore; new DPSUs (ex-OFB) ₹19,551 crore; non-DPSUs ₹6,774 crore; private companies ₹26,675 crore; total ₹1,27,434 crore; defence licences 215 (2014) → 728 (Dec 2024) [documented]

Service pay-and-allowances actual (three services, excluding civilians and Agnipath): 2009-10 ₹45,100.85 cr; 2013-14 ₹61,625.32 cr; 2024-25 ₹143,311.23 cr (₹150,770.98 cr with Agnipath) [documented, summed]

DAC Acceptance-of-Necessity (AoN) approvals as PIB prints them (an AoN approves the need and the category, not a vendor — vendor not named): 2022-03-22 ₹8,357 crore, all Buy (Indian-IDDM), plus ₹380.43 crore consolidated AoN for iDEX start-ups/MSMEs [documented]

2023: January ₹4,276 crore; March over ₹70,500 crore (BrahMos, Shakti EW, utility helicopters-maritime ₹56,000 crore for the Navy; ATAGS with gun-towing vehicles; ALH Mk-III for the Coast Guard); June 31 MQ-9B via US FMS (value not stated); July 26 Rafale-Marine from France under an IGA; August about ₹7,800 crore; 2023-09-15 about ₹45,000 crore (nine proposals incl. 12 Su-30MKI); 2023-11-30 ₹2.23 lakh crore of which ₹2.20 lakh crore (98%) from domestic industry (incl. LCH and LCA Mk1A from HAL, Su-30 upgrade, towed gun system); calendar 2023 total over ₹3.50 lakh crore [documented, PIB YER 2023, PIB 1957703, PIB 1981135]

2024: February ₹84,560 crore; September ₹1,44,716 crore; 2024-12-03 over ₹21,772 crore; PIB YER 2024: to November 2024, 40 proposals ₹4,22,129.55 crore of which ₹3,97,584.34 crore (94.19%) from indigenous sources [documented]

2025: 2025-03-20 over ₹54,000 crore; 2025-07-03 about ₹1.05 lakh crore (10 proposals, indigenous); 2025-08-05 about ₹67,000 crore; 2025-10-23 about ₹79,000 crore; 2025-12-29 about ₹79,000 crore; since January 2025 over ₹3.84 lakh crore (PIB YER 2025, a calendar-year window) [documented]

FY2025-26 (PIB 2026-03-27): AoN for 55 proposals ₹6.73 lakh crore and capital contracts signed for 503 proposals ₹2.28 lakh crore — 'both ... the highest in any given Financial Year'. 2026-02-12: AoN of about ₹3.60 lakh crore incl. the Multi Role Fighter Aircraft (Rafale; the ministry: 'the majority of MRFA to be procured will be manufactured in India'), P-8I and Dornier EO/IR; 2026-03-27 about ₹2.38 lakh crore (S-400, Medium Transport Aircraft, Dhanush, Remotely Piloted Strike Aircraft) [documented; Feb 2026 via AIR]

claims.lab: Government of India holds 63.33% of Cochin Shipyard Limited after the July 2026 offer for sale
claims.d: The President of India acting through the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways sold 1,20,49,170 equity shares of Cochin Shipyard on 7 and 8 July 2026 by offer for sale through the stock exchange mechanism, aggregating ₹1,713.28 crore. Primary record: the promoter's Form B under SEBI PIT Reg 7(2)(a), dated 9 Jul 2026 and signed for MoPSW by its Director, forwarded by the company to BSE/NSE on 10 Jul 2026 under Reg 7(2)(b); it prints holdings prior 17,86,71,239 shares (67.91%), disposed 1,20,49,170 (sale, ₹1,713.28 crore), held post 16,66,22,069 (63.33%), ISIN INE704P01025. On the 30 Jun 2026 filing's 26,30,80,780 shares, of which the promoter held 17,86,71,239 (67.91%), the sale leaves 16,66,22,069 shares, per the promoter's Form B (63.33%), matching this file's computation. The OFS notice of 6 Jul 2026 offered a base 66,29,636 shares (2.52%) with an equal oversubscription option, exercised by the 7 Jul 2026 notice (offer up to 1,32,59,272 shares, 5.04%); 1,20,49,170 were sold. Effective 8 Jul 2026 (last OFS day); 'from' is recorded at month precision. Business Standard's 10 Jul 2026 item is an unbylined capital-market wire note ('No Business Standard Journalist was involved') and is secondary corroboration only. Supersedes union-defence:c016.

claims.lab: Defence (four demands) as % of GDP fell from 3.32% (BE 2000-01) to 2.00% (BE 2026-27); actuals 2.83% (2009-10) → 1.92% (2024-25)
claims.d: Numerator: Defence Services (Revenue) + Capital Outlay + Defence Pensions + MoD Civil as the demands print them (pre-2016-17 the revenue figure is the sum of the per-service demands). Denominator: GDP at current prices, Economic Survey 2025-26 Statistical Appendix Table 1.6 (2011-12 series) and, for 2026-27, the Budget at a Glance projection. SIPRI, which adds the CAPFs and uses its own GDP, prints 2.22% for 2024 and 2.30% for 2025. Numerator notes: the BE 2000-01 total nets the Defence Ordnance Factories demand (Demand 18, −₹215.04 crore) as the demands print it; BE 2000-01 was the post-Kargil step-up year, so the 3.32% start is a local peak (a BE 2001-02 or BE 2004-05 start gives 3.16% / 2.80%, a smaller fall). Denominator notes: GDP before 2011-12 is the Economic Survey's spliced back-series in Table 1.6, not MoSPI's official back-series (which starts in 2004-05) — pre-2004-05 values are linked estimates and the 3.32% carries extra error; the 2026-27 denominator is the Budget at a Glance projection of 10% nominal growth over the 2025-26 First Advance Estimates, not an NSO estimate; MoSPI released a new GDP series on base 2022-23 in Feb 2026, which revises 2022-23 onward, so the 1.92% / 2.00% endpoints will move slightly once the Survey and BaG adopt it.

claims.lab: UPA-II vs NDA on identical fields: nominal CAGR of the MoD total 11.0% vs 8.8%; real 2.5% vs 4.4%; average pension share 15.6% vs 23.3%; capital share 33.8% vs 26.6%
claims.d: Same lens, both governments, Budget Estimates of the four MoD demands summed. UPA-II (BE 2009-10→2013-14): average shares revenue 48.6% / capital 33.8% / pensions 15.6% / MoD civil 2.1%; nominal CAGR of the MoD total 11.0% (GDP at current prices grew 15.3% a year), real CAGR 2.5% deflating by the GNI implicit deflator (Economic Survey 2025-26 Table 1.1). NDA (BE 2014-15→2026-27): average shares revenue 45.3% / capital 26.6% / pensions 23.3% / civil 4.7%; nominal CAGR 8.8% (GDP 10.0%), real CAGR 4.4% over 2014-15→2025-26 (no deflator yet for 2026-27); the first five NDA years alone: nominal 9.1%, real 5.6%. Pay-to-capital (uniformed Pay & Allowances of the three services ÷ Capital Outlay demand, BE): 2000-01 0.71; 2001-02 0.68; 2004-05 0.46; 2005-06 0.47; 2008-09 0.39; 2009-10 0.71; 2010-11 0.67; 2011-12 0.63; 2013-14 0.67; 2014-15 0.71; 2016-17 1.08; 2017-18 1.10; 2018-19 1.10; 2019-20 1.05; 2020-21 1.03; 2021-22 0.87; 2022-23 0.88; 2023-24 0.85; 2024-25 0.85; 2025-26 0.81; 2026-27 0.68. Reading: under both governments the budget grew a little faster than nominal GDP in some years and slower in others, and the pension share rose under both — the step changes are the 2008-09/2009-10 Sixth Pay Commission arrears and OROP (UPA-II and early NDA), the 7th CPC from 2016-17 (NDA), and the RE 2025-26 spectrum-charges line (NDA). The capital share fell under UPA-II and stayed in the high twenties under NDA; the revenue share is the mirror. Neither record is a scandal: both are the arithmetic of a manpower-heavy force paying pensions out of the same envelope. The 2016-17 budget moved Ordnance Factories and R&D (revenue and capital) into the MoD (Misc) demand for one year, which inflates 'civil' and deflates 'revenue' for BE 2015-16/2016-17 in these averages; the four-demand total is unaffected. Method notes: the real CAGR deflates by the GNI implicit deflator (Economic Survey Table 1.1) while the GDP comparator is nominal GDP (Table 1.6). The Feb 2014 interim BE 2014-15 (₹2,79,202.87 crore, UPA-II) was replaced by the July 2014 NDA BE (₹2,85,202.87 crore); each window leaves out its government's first-budget increment, and including them gives 15.4% against 9.1% with the ordering unchanged (audit computation). BE 2026-27 includes ₹37,200 crore of spectrum charges; ex-spectrum the NDA nominal CAGR is about 8.4%.

claims.d: Share computed from the budgets rows. Pensions actual 2009-10 ₹34,999.45 crore against BE ₹21,790.00 crore (Sixth CPC arrears); actual 2022-23 ₹153,406.90 crore against BE ₹119,696.00 crore (OROP revision arrears); BE 2026-27 ₹171,338.22 crore, +6.6% over BE 2025-26. claims.d: Capital Outlay on Defence Services is the acquisition-plus-works demand; BE 2026-27 ₹219,306.47 crore is +17.6% over RE 2025-26 ₹186,454.20 crore (27.95% of the net four-demand total; printed as 27.9%). Real growth is BE-to-BE: ₹54,824 crore (BE 2009-10) → ₹86,740.71 crore (BE 2013-14), and ₹94,587.95 crore (BE 2014-15) → ₹180,000 crore (BE 2025-26); against RE 2025-26 (₹186,454.20 crore) the NDA figure is about 2.5% a year, and BE 2014-15 sits above BE 2015-16 (₹85,894.44 crore) and BE 2016-17 (₹78,586.68 crore), so the 2014-15 base flatters nothing. Capital actuals fell short of BE in 2024-25 (₹159,768.40 vs ₹172,000.00 crore) and exceeded BE in 2018-19 (₹95,230.59 vs ₹93,982.13 crore) and 2020-21 (₹134,304.92 vs ₹113,734.00 crore). Scope break: the 2016-17 document moved Ordnance Factories and R&D capital into the MoD (Misc) demand, so BE 2015-16, RE 2015-16 and BE 2016-17 (₹78,586.68 crore) and the actual 2014-15 printed there (₹73,401.04 crore; the Misc demand carries OF ₹746.19 + R&D ₹7,482.52 crore for that year) exclude them, while the 2018-19 document's actual 2016-17 (₹86,356.93 crore) includes OF ₹716.70 + R&D ₹6,771.50 crore — like-for-like 2016-17 exceeds BE by only ₹282 crore, and the 2014-15 shortfall is ₹12,958 crore like-for-like, not ₹21,187 crore. The 2000-01 share nets the Demand 18 Ordnance Factories figure (−₹215.04 crore) in the denominator (the budgets rows cannot carry a negative figure; the void records it), which is why the rows alone give 25.2%.

claims.d: SIPRI figures for India include the BSF, CRPF, Assam Rifles, ITBP and (from 2007) SSB and exclude military nuclear activities (footnote 59), so they run above the MoD-demand ratio in this file; coverage differs for the peers too — Pakistan's series includes paramilitary forces and pensions (footnote 60), the US figure includes part of the National Intelligence Program and Ukraine aid (footnote 44), and SIPRI's China figure is its own upward estimate above the official budget (footnote 55). Share of general government spending 2024: India 7.6%, China 5.1%, Pakistan 14.0%, US 9.0%, UK 5.6%. The 2025 column in the same file gives India 2.30%; 2024 is used because it is the last year with a full peer set. The World Bank WDI series is corroborating only — an older SIPRI vintage on a World Bank GDP denominator — and prints different 2024 values (India 2.27, China 1.71, Pakistan 2.67, US 3.42, UK 2.28).

narratives.strongestCase: The four-demand ratio to GDP fell from 3.32% (BE 2000-01) to 2.00% (BE 2026-27) and the share of Union expenditure from about 17% (2014-15) to 14.7% (BE 2026-27, PRS); the Standing Committee on Defence (2018) asked for about 3% of GDP; China spends 3.6× India in constant dollars.
narratives.strongestCounter: India was SIPRI's fifth-largest spender in 2025 (US$93.3bn constant 2024, SIPRI v1.2) and sixth in 2024 in the v1.2 file, behind the UK at 89.8bn (PRS's 'fifth highest in 2024' reflects SIPRI's April 2025 release, which v1.2 superseded); its ratio (2.22% of GDP, SIPRI 2024) is above China's (1.66%), France's (2.01%) and Germany's (1.84%) but below the UK's (2.44%), the US's (3.43%) and Pakistan's (2.73%) (SIPRI v1.2, 2024). The Ministry of Finance's position (quoted by PRS) is that allocation follows need and resources, not a fixed share. In rupees the four demands grew 8.8% a year 2014-15→2026-27 (PRS sets this against central expenditure growth of 10.2%) against GDP growth of 10.0% (this file's own CAGR from Economic Survey Table 1.6 and the BAG 2026-27 projection); under UPA-II (BE 2009-10→2013-14) the same demands grew 11.0% a year against GDP growth of 15.3%: the ratio fell under both governments, and the fall is the denominator. Innocent reading: a falling ratio is what a fast-growing denominator does to any budget line held roughly constant in real terms; it says nothing about adequacy without a costed threat assessment.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A costed force-structure requirement (the Standing Committee's projected-vs-allocated tables, or an LTIPP) showing a persistent gap in actuals, not in BE; or a GDP-neutral measure such as spend per serving soldier against peers.

narratives.claim: Pensions are eating the defence budget.
narratives.strongestCase: Defence Pensions rose from 16.9% of the MoD total (BE 2000-01; PRS prints 16% on a slightly different denominator) to a peak of 28.4% (BE 2020-21) and stands at 21.8% in BE 2026-27 (₹171,338.22 crore, net; PIB: 21.84%), close to the whole Demand 21 Capital Outlay on Defence Services (₹2,19,306.47 crore; PRS's ₹2,31,010 crore adds MoD (Civil) capital); salaries and pensions together are 44% of BE 2026-27 (PRS). Stage note: BE 2025-26 and BE 2026-27 pensions are net of a ₹8,000 crore 'Deduct Recovery from Public Account' that BE 2020-21 does not carry; gross BE 2026-27 is ₹179,338.22 crore, about 22.6% of the gross four-demand total.
narratives.strongestCounter: The share has fallen back from its 2020-21 peak as the end of OROP-revision arrears and faster growth of capital (+21.8%) and revenue (+17.2%) in the denominator slow it: pension BE 2026-27 is +6.6% over BE 2025-26 net-on-net (6.24% gross-on-gross per the demand note; +1.3% over RE 2025-26, PRS 'growth of 1%'). Agnipath's pension effect (75% of each cohort exits without a pension, PRS) lies years ahead and is not in these numbers. Pensions are a contract with people who already served; the 'eating' metaphor treats a liability as a choice. The claim holds for 2000-01→2020-21 and is contested for the years since.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A pensioner head-count and average-pension series (DESW) that separates volume from rate; the first Agnipath cohort reaching four years in 2026-27 and the Ministry's stated saving being tested in RE.

narratives.strongestCase: Capital Outlay's share of the MoD total fell from a one-year peak of 37.6% (BE 2004-05; 25.3% in BE 2000-01) to 33.2% (BE 2014-15) and 27.9% (BE 2026-27); actuals fell short of BE in 2022-23 (₹142,940.01 vs ₹152,369.61 crore), 2023-24 (₹154,256.28 vs ₹162,600 crore, PRS) and 2024-25 (₹159,768.40 vs ₹172,000 crore, a ₹12,232 crore gap). The Standing Committee on Defence (3rd Report, Dec 2019; PRS Table 6) found committed liabilities exceeding the modernisation budget by 15% (2016-17), 25%, 33% and 29% (2019-20); the tables have not been disclosed since 2019-20. PRS: capital expenditure averaged 27% of the defence budget against the 40% the Standing Committee recommended in 2021 (60:40).
narratives.strongestCounter: In rupees the capital demand went from ₹54,824 crore (BE 2009-10) to ₹219,306.47 crore (BE 2026-27), +17.6% over RE 2025-26 (Demand 21: ₹186,454.20 → ₹219,306.47 crore; PRS's 17% is on its broader ₹1,97,417 → ₹2,31,010 crore aggregate), and in real terms (GNI deflator, BE-to-BE) grew 2.2% a year 2014-15→2025-26 — a lower bound, since the BE 2014-15 base was heavily underspent (actual ₹73,401.04 crore on a narrower scope); PRS gives about 9% nominal 2014-15→2026-27. Actuals exceeded BE in 2018-19 (₹95,230.59 vs ₹93,982.13 crore) and 2020-21 (₹134,304.92 vs ₹113,734.00 crore); 2016-17 exceeds BE by only ₹282 crore like-for-like (the printed actual ₹86,356.93 crore includes ₹7,488.20 crore of Ordnance Factories and R&D capital that BE 2016-17 ₹78,586.68 crore booked under the MoD (Misc) demand). The Ministry said on 2 Apr 2026 that the RE 2025-26 capital of ₹1.86 lakh crore was fully used; actual 2024-25 ≈ RE 2024-25 (₹159,500 crore), so the ₹12,232 crore gap was a cut made at the RE stage, not a surrender. The share fell because pensions, pay and in 2025-26 spectrum charges grew inside the same envelope. Innocent reading: capital outlay is lumpy, and a lower share with a higher rupee figure is not a collapse.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The committed-liability test is already met for 2016-17→2019-20 (Standing Committee, Dec 2019). The open question is whether the post-2019-20 committed-liability tables, undisclosed so far, show the shortfall persisting against the modernisation balance; a multi-year run of capital actuals below RE with surrendered funds (CAG paragraphs on unspent capital) would move this to well-supported, a disclosed run of liabilities within the balance to unsupported.

symmetryCheck: Same lens, both governments, Budget Estimates of the four MoD demands summed. UPA-II (BE 2009-10→2013-14): average shares revenue 48.6% / capital 33.8% / pensions 15.6% / MoD civil 2.1%; nominal CAGR of the MoD total 11.0% (GDP at current prices grew 15.3% a year), real CAGR 2.5% deflating by the GNI implicit deflator (Economic Survey 2025-26 Table 1.1). NDA (BE 2014-15→2026-27): average shares revenue 45.3% / capital 26.6% / pensions 23.3% / civil 4.7%; nominal CAGR 8.8% (GDP 10.0%), real CAGR 4.4% over 2014-15→2025-26 (no deflator yet for 2026-27); the first five NDA years alone: nominal 9.1%, real 5.6%. Pay-to-capital (uniformed Pay & Allowances of the three services ÷ Capital Outlay demand, BE): 2000-01 0.71; 2001-02 0.68; 2004-05 0.46; 2005-06 0.47; 2008-09 0.39; 2009-10 0.71; 2010-11 0.67; 2011-12 0.63; 2013-14 0.67; 2014-15 0.71; 2016-17 1.08; 2017-18 1.10; 2018-19 1.10; 2019-20 1.05; 2020-21 1.03; 2021-22 0.87; 2022-23 0.88; 2023-24 0.85; 2024-25 0.85; 2025-26 0.81; 2026-27 0.68. Reading: under both governments the budget grew a little faster than nominal GDP in some years and slower in others, and the pension share rose under both — the step changes are the 2008-09/2009-10 Sixth Pay Commission arrears and OROP (UPA-II and early NDA), the 7th CPC from 2016-17 (NDA), and the RE 2025-26 spectrum-charges line (NDA). The capital share fell under UPA-II and stayed in the high twenties under NDA; the revenue share is the mirror. Neither record is a scandal: both are the arithmetic of a manpower-heavy force paying pensions out of the same envelope. The 2016-17 budget moved Ordnance Factories and R&D (revenue and capital) into the MoD (Misc) demand for one year, which inflates 'civil' and deflates 'revenue' for BE 2015-16/2016-17 in these averages; the four-demand total is unaffected.

gaps: Actuals for FY2001-02, 2002-03, 2003-04, 2005-06, 2006-07, 2007-08, 2010-11, 2011-12, 2013-14, 2015-16, 2017-18, 2019-20, 2021-22, 2023-24 and RE for 2001-02, 2002-03, 2003-04, 2005-06, 2006-07, 2007-08, 2011-12, 2012-13: they sit in the odd-year Notes on Demands (e.g. indiabudget.gov.in/budget2025-26/doc/eb/sbe20.pdf for actual 2023-24) which the fetch budget did not reach; the Summary of Demands for those years is BE-only (and image-only PDFs for 2013-14 and 2015-16).

Pay & Allowances for BE/RE 2015-16 and actual 2014-15: the 2016-17 document prints them in a second, old-structure block that the extractor did not read; BE 2012-13 pay is absent because only the Summary was fetched for that year.
Government holding in Hindustan Shipyard Ltd and Goa Shipyard Ltd (unlisted; GSL is majority-held by Mazagon Dock) was not verified; the DDP Annual Report 2024-25 states only BEML's 54% in words.

Registered-office states of the seven ex-OFB companies are given from their public identity (MIL Pune, AVNL Chennai, AWEIL/TCL/GIL Kanpur, YIL Nagpur, IOL Dehradun) and were not fetched; the companies' own pages or MCA would confirm.

Ministers' tenure dates come from Wikipedia (reported); mod.gov.in and the Cabinet Secretariat notifications were not reachable; a PIB release on the Cabinet approval of OFB corporatisation (16 Jun 2021) was not located (two guessed PRIDs resolved to unrelated releases and are not cited).

Total Union expenditure for BE 2015-16, 2019-20 to 2024-25 and actuals 2011-12, 2013-14, 2014-15 was not collected (the Budget at a Glance for those years was not fetched), so the %-of-Union-expenditure base rate is missing for those (fy, stage) pairs.
GDP uses the 2011-12 series with the Economic Survey's back-cast for 1996-97→2013-14 and the Budget projection for 2026-27; MoSPI's own press note was not fetched (404 on the guessed path).
The CAPFs that SIPRI adds to India's figure are in the union-home domain, not here; a reconciled all-force ratio needs both files.

BSE shareholding-pattern API (api.bseindia.com) returned Access Denied on 2026-10-04 (audit); the NSE corporate-share-holdings-master API and its XBRL files were used instead for all eight listed PSUs.

The Week article of 8 Jul 2026 on the Cochin Shipyard OFS (theweek.in) returned Access Denied through the proxy and is not cited; Business Standard (10 Jul 2026) carries the same company announcement.

mod.gov.in/en/former-defence-ministers returned 503 on 2026-10-04; PIB take-over releases were opened for 2004, 2006, 2014, 2017, 2019 and 2024, so the roster rests on PIB plus two outlets for 2001 and 2017; a Rashtrapati Bhavan communiqué was opened for none of them.
The Standing Committee on Defence committed-liability tables (3rd Report, Dec 2019) are cited through PRS Table 6; the report itself and any later table were not opened.
